questions.text: What is Laravel?
options: A proprietary PHP content management system
An open-source PHP web application framework
questions.explanation: Slide: "Laravel is an open-source PHP web application framework."

questions.text: Who created Laravel?
questions.explanation: Laravel was created by Taylor Otwell. (Rasmus Lerdorf created PHP itself, Fabien Potencier created Symfony, and Jeffrey Way runs Laracasts.)

questions.text: In what year was Laravel created?
questions.explanation: Slide: "Created by Taylor Otwell in 2011."

questions.text: Which architectural pattern does Laravel follow?
questions.explanation: Laravel follows the Model-View-Controller (MVC) architectural pattern.

questions.text: In MVC, the letters stand for Model, ___, and Controller.
questions.explanation: MVC = Model-View-Controller.

questions.text: According to the slides, what does Laravel aim to do?
options: Replace PHP with a compiled language
Remove the need for a database
Make websites run without a web server
Make web development easier and more elegant
questions.explanation: Slide: Laravel "aims to make web development easier and more elegant."

questions.text: Laravel is an open-source framework.
questions.explanation: Laravel is open-source (free to use and modify).

questions.text: What is Laravel's official website, as given on the slides?
questions.explanation: The slide links to https://laravel.com/.

questions.text: Why do Laravel developers use a framework like Laravel instead of writing custom projects completely from scratch?
options: Laravel code runs without PHP installed
Frameworks are required by PHP to run at all
Writing everything from scratch could take ages; a framework saves time
questions.explanation: Slide: "writing the code from scratch in custom projects could take ages, so a framework like Laravel is used to save time."

questions.text: Match each "Why Laravel?" feature to its description.
allChoices: Authentication, role authorization, email verification, password hashing
Easily create and maintain lightweight templates for web pages
Add ready-made features without writing code from scratch
Write database queries using PHP syntax rather than SQL
Use simple names instead of long path names; change them in one place
Easier to manage thanks to version control

pairs.match: Add ready-made features without writing code from scratch
Use simple names instead of long path names; change them in one place
Authentication, role authorization, email verification, password hashing
Easier to manage thanks to version control
Easily create and maintain lightweight templates for web pages
Write database queries using PHP syntax rather than SQL

questions.explanation: These are the six features from the two "Why Laravel?" slides.

questions.text: What does Eloquent ORM let developers do?
options: Automatically design database schemas from HTML forms
Write front-end components in PHP instead of JavaScript
Write database queries using PHP syntax rather than SQL code
questions.explanation: Slide: "Developers can write database queries using PHP syntax rather than SQL code. This makes it faster to manage and query databases."

questions.text: ORM stands for Object ___ Mapping.
questions.explanation: ORM = Object Relational Mapping (Eloquent is Laravel's ORM).

questions.text: Which of these are listed on the slides as Laravel security features? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Slide: "Laravel offers a range of security features, such as user authentication, role authorizations, email verifications, password hashing and more."

questions.text: According to the "Route Handling" feature, what makes bigger applications easier to manage?
options: Hard-coding full URLs everywhere in the app
Putting every route inside its own controller
Using simple route names instead of long path names, changeable in one dedicated file
questions.explanation: Slide: "Using simple names, rather than long path names makes it easier to manage bigger applications. Plus all route names can be changed in one place via a dedicated file…"

questions.text: According to the slides, what makes database migrations much easier to manage?
questions.explanation: Slide: "With version control, database migrations are much easier to manage."

questions.text: What does the Blade template engine let developers do, according to the "Why Laravel?" slide?
options: Write SQL queries in PHP syntax
Easily create and maintain lightweight templates for their web pages
questions.explanation: Slide: "The Blade template engine allows developers to easily create and maintain lightweight templates for their web pages."

questions.text: What does having built-in modules (built-in packages) mean?
options: Every feature must be written manually
You must buy each module separately
You can add ready-made features to your app without writing code from scratch
Laravel can only be used offline
questions.explanation: Slide: "Built-in packages mean that you can add ready-made features to your web application, without the need of having to write code from scratch."

questions.text: According to the lecture notes, because of its extensive list of powerful features, Laravel is recommended for big projects rather than small, simple web projects.
questions.explanation: Speaker notes: "Because Laravel has an extensive list of powerful features, it is recommended to be used on big projects, rather than small, simple web projects."

questions.text: Which of the following are listed under Key Features of Laravel? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Key Features slide: clean and elegant syntax, built-in authentication & authorization, Eloquent ORM, Blade templating engine, Artisan CLI for automation, and Routing/Middleware/Caching.

questions.text: What is Artisan?
questions.explanation: Artisan is the CLI (php artisan …) — listed as "Artisan CLI for automation" on the Key Features slide.

questions.text: Which of these is Laravel's database-handling tool listed on the Key Features slide?
questions.explanation: "Eloquent ORM for database handling." Blade = templating, Artisan = CLI, Composer = dependency manager.

questions.text: According to the salary slide, what is the total monthly pay range for a PHP Laravel Developer in the Philippines?
questions.explanation: The slide shows a total pay range of ₱24K – ₱106K/mo.

questions.text: According to the same salary slide, what is the median total pay for a PHP Laravel Developer in the Philippines?
questions.explanation: The slide shows ₱43K/mo median total pay.

questions.text: On the job-listings slide, which company showed the highest pay for a PHP Laravel Developer?
questions.explanation: ConnectOS listed ₱120K – ₱132K/mo total pay (₱126K median).

questions.text: What is the minimum PHP version listed as a prerequisite for a Laravel development environment?
questions.explanation: Prerequisites slide: "PHP >= 8.1".

questions.text: Which of these are listed as prerequisites for setting up a Laravel development environment? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Prerequisites: PHP >= 8.1, Composer, MySQL or any supported DB, a web server (Apache/Nginx) or Laravel Sail (Docker), an IDE, and Node.

questions.text: Why is Node listed as a prerequisite?
options: To compile your application's frontend assets
questions.explanation: Slide: "Node (compile your application's frontend assets.)"

questions.text: Laravel Sail is listed as an alternative to Apache/Nginx. What technology is it based on?
questions.explanation: Slide: "Web server (Apache/Nginx) or Laravel Sail (Docker)".

questions.text: Which web servers are named on the prerequisites slide?
questions.explanation: Slide: "Web server (Apache/Nginx) or Laravel Sail (Docker)".

questions.text: Which IDEs are given as examples on the prerequisites slide?
questions.explanation: Slide: "IDE (e.g., VS Code, PHPStorm)".

questions.text: What is Composer?
options: A tool at the foundation of most modern PHP development (a PHP dependency manager)
questions.explanation: Slide: "Composer is a tool that's at the foundation of most modern PHP development."

questions.text: According to the slides, what is Composer used for with Laravel? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Slide: "Composer to install Laravel, update Laravel, and bring in external dependencies." Migrations and generating controllers are done with Artisan; Blade compiles its own templates.

questions.text: Complete the command that creates a new Laravel project using Composer.
questions.explanation: composer create-project laravel/laravel projectName — Composer's create-project creates a new project from a skeleton.

questions.text: Complete the two commands for the Laravel Installer method.
questions.explanation: First install the installer globally with composer global require "laravel/installer", then create a project with laravel new projectName.

questions.text: Composer's create-project feature creates new projects with a particular…
questions.explanation: Slide: "Composer offers a feature called create-project for creating new projects with a particular skeleton."

questions.text: You run composer create-project laravel/laravel blog. What happens?
options: A new subdirectory named blog is created in your current directory containing a new Laravel project
Nothing — you must run laravel new blog first
A project is created directly in your current directory with no subfolder
questions.explanation: Slide: "this will create a subdirectory of your current directory named {projectName}".

questions.text: What must you have before you can install the Laravel installer tool?
questions.explanation: Slide: "If you have Composer installed globally, install the Laravel installer tool is as simple as running…"

questions.text: Both the composer create-project method and the laravel new method create a new subdirectory named after the project in your current directory.
questions.explanation: Both slides say the command creates a subdirectory of your current directory named {projectName}.

questions.text: Which command installs the Laravel installer tool?
questions.explanation: The installer is a global Composer package: composer global require "laravel/installer".

questions.text: Once the installer is installed, which command spins up a new Laravel project named shop?
questions.explanation: Slide: "laravel new projectName".

questions.text: Match each MVC component to its role.
allChoices: Connects Model and View and contains the business logic
The user interface; everything the user sees on screen
Interacts with the database

pairs.match: The user interface; everything the user sees on screen
Connects Model and View and contains the business logic

questions.explanation: From the MVC slide.

questions.text: Which MVC component is called the "Heart of the application"?
questions.explanation: Slide: the Controller "is also known as the 'Heart of the application in MVC'."

questions.text: Which MVC component interacts with the database?
questions.explanation: Slide: "Model: It interacts with the database."

questions.text: Which MVC component contains everything a user can see on the screen?
questions.explanation: Slide: "View: User Interface. It contains everything which a user can see on the screen."

questions.text: Which MVC component contains all the business logic?
questions.explanation: Slide: "Controller: It helps to connect Model and View and contains all the business logic."

questions.text: In the MVC diagram on the slides, which component does the user interact with directly?
questions.explanation: The diagram shows the user connected to the View with a "User Interact" arrow.

questions.text: In the MVC diagram, the Controller sends "Rendering data" to which component?
questions.explanation: The "Rendering data" arrow goes from the Controller to the View.

questions.text: In the MVC diagram, what is the label of the arrow going from the View to the Controller?
questions.explanation: View → Controller is "Response From User"; Controller → View is "Rendering data".

questions.text: In the MVC diagram, when the Controller needs data, it sends "Request Data" to which component?
questions.explanation: Controller → Model is "Request Data"; Model → Controller is "Response Data".

questions.text: In the MVC diagram, which component exchanges "Requesting Data" / "Responsing Data" with the database?
questions.explanation: Only the Model is connected to the database in the diagram.

questions.text: In the MVC diagram, the View communicates directly with the database.
questions.explanation: The View only talks to the user and the Controller. Only the Model talks to the database.

questions.text: Which are listed as advantages of using an MVC framework? (Select all that apply)
options: Helps in a faster development process
Removes the need for a database
Removes the need for a web server
questions.explanation: Advantages slide: organizing large-scale projects, easier modification, a change in one part won't affect the others, faster development, and Asynchronous Method Invocation.

questions.text: One listed advantage of MVC is that a modification in one part won't affect any other part of the code.
questions.explanation: Advantages slide: "Modification in any part won't affect any other part of the code."

questions.text: Drag each MVC piece to the folder where it lives in a Laravel project.
questions.explanation: From the study plan (Session 1.3): Models → app/Models, Views → resources/views, Controllers → app/Http/Controllers.

questions.text: Drag each description to the correct Laravel folder (part 1).

pairs.match: Core code; almost all of your application's classes
All of your application's configuration files
index.php entry point; images, JavaScript, CSS

questions.explanation: From the Laravel Folder Structure slides.

questions.text: Drag each description to the correct Laravel folder (part 2).

pairs.match: Logs, compiled Blade templates, file sessions, file caches

questions.explanation: From the Laravel Folder Structure slides.

questions.text: Which directory contains the index.php file?
questions.explanation: Slide: "The public directory contains the index.php file…"

questions.text: What is the role of public/index.php?
options: It is the entry point for all requests entering your application and configures autoloading
questions.explanation: Slide: "…the index.php file, which is the entry point for all requests entering your application and configures autoloading."

questions.text: Both public and resources hold CSS/JavaScript. According to the slides, what's the difference?
options: resources holds raw, un-compiled assets; public houses the assets that are served (images, JS, CSS)
There is no difference; they are duplicates
public holds raw, un-compiled assets; resources holds compiled ones
questions.explanation: resources: "your views as well as your raw, un-compiled assets such as CSS or JavaScript". public: "houses your assets such as images, JavaScript, and CSS."

questions.text: Which directory contains your logs, compiled Blade templates, file-based sessions, and file caches?
questions.explanation: Slide: "The storage directory contains your logs, compiled Blade templates, file based sessions, file caches, and other files generated by the framework."

questions.text: Which directory contains your database migrations, model factories, and seeds?
questions.explanation: Slide: "The database directory contains your database migrations, model factories, and seeds."

questions.text: Which directory contains the core code of your application, where almost all of your classes live?
questions.explanation: Slide: "The app directory contains the core code of your application. Almost all of the classes in your application will be in this directory."

questions.text: Which directory contains your Composer dependencies?
questions.explanation: Slide: "The vendor directory contains your Composer dependencies."

questions.text: Which testing tools do the slides say Laravel's tests directory provides examples for out of the box?
questions.explanation: Slide: "Example Pest or PHPUnit unit tests and feature tests are provided out of the box."

questions.text: According to the Folder Structure slide, which two route files are included with Laravel by default?
questions.explanation: Slide: "By default, two route files are included with Laravel: web.php and console.php." (The Routes deck also mentions routes/api.php for API routes. In Laravel 11 that file isn't created by default; you add it with php artisan install:api.)

questions.text: Laravel strictly forces you to put each class in one specific folder.
questions.explanation: Slide: "Laravel imposes almost no restrictions on where any given class is located - as long as Composer can autoload the class."

questions.text: According to the slides, what is the only real requirement for where a class can be located in a Laravel app?
options: It must be in the vendor folder
Composer must be able to autoload the class
It must be inside the app/Http folder
questions.explanation: Laravel imposes almost no restrictions "as long as Composer can autoload the class."

questions.text: Which directory contains all of your application's configuration files?
questions.explanation: Slide: "The config directory, as the name implies, contains all of your application's configuration files."

questions.text: The default Laravel folder structure is meant to be a good starting point for both large and small applications.
questions.explanation: Slide: "The default Laravel application structure is intended to provide a great starting point for both large and small applications."

questions.text: What is routing?
options: The process of migrating the database
The process of installing Composer packages
The process of directing an incoming request to a specific controller method
The process of compiling Blade templates
questions.explanation: Slide: "Routing is the process of directing an incoming request to a specific controller method."

questions.text: In Laravel, what do routes define?
options: The PHP version the app requires
The CSS styles of each page
The URLs your application can respond to and how they are handled
questions.explanation: Slide: "In Laravel, routes define the URLs your application can respond to and how they are handled."

questions.text: Routes let you handle HTTP requests and send appropriate responses.
questions.explanation: Slide: "They allow you to handle HTTP requests and send appropriate responses."

questions.text: According to the Basic Routing slide, where are these routes defined?
allChoices: routes/api.php
app/routes.php
routes/web.php
routes/console.php
questions.explanation: Slide: "Routes are defined in the routes/web.php file for web routes and routes/api.php for API routes."

questions.text: Match each part of this basic route to what it means: Route::get('/welcome', function () { return view('welcome'); });
allChoices: Defines a route that responds to a GET request
The URL path
A closure that returns a response

pairs.match: Defines a route that responds to a GET request
A closure that returns a response

questions.explanation: From the Basic Routing slide.

questions.text: Complete the basic GET route from the slides.
questions.explanation: Route::get defines a route that responds to a GET request.

questions.text: In the basic route example, what does return view('welcome'); do?
options: Creates a new view file named welcome
questions.explanation: The view() helper renders a view by name; 'welcome' maps to resources/views/welcome.blade.php.

questions.text: In the route Route::get('/welcome', function () { ... }), the function () { ... } is an anonymous function. What is it called in PHP/Laravel?
questions.explanation: The slide calls it a "Closure that returns a response." A closure is an anonymous function.

questions.text: HTTP verbs are also known as…
questions.explanation: Slide: "HTTP verbs, also known as HTTP methods, are used to indicate the desired action to be performed on a given resource."

questions.text: Match each HTTP verb to what it does (as described on the slides).
allChoices: Delete a resource
Modify a resource or update data
Request a resource (or list of resources) / retrieve data
Create a resource or submit data
Overwrite a resource or update data

pairs.match: Request a resource (or list of resources) / retrieve data
Create a resource or submit data
Overwrite a resource or update data
Modify a resource or update data

questions.explanation: From the HTTP Verbs overview slide.

questions.text: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH according to the slides?
options: PUT deletes a resource; PATCH creates one
PUT overwrites a resource; PATCH modifies it
PUT retrieves data; PATCH submits data
There is no difference; they are aliases
questions.explanation: PUT = "Overwrite a resource or update data"; PATCH = "Modify a resource or update data".

questions.text: Which HTTP verb should you use to create a resource or submit data?
questions.explanation: POST: "Create a resource or submit data."

questions.text: Which HTTP verb should you use to retrieve a list of resources?
questions.explanation: GET: "Request a resource (or a list of resources) or retrieve data."

questions.text: Typing a URL into a browser's address bar sends a GET request.
questions.explanation: The study plan notes that browsers only issue GET when you type a URL, which is why POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE routes need a form, curl, Postman, or tinker to test.

questions.text: You defined Route::post('/items', ...). Per the study plan, which command lets you test it from the terminal?
questions.explanation: curl -X POST sends a POST request. Plain curl sends a GET.

questions.text: Complete the routes so each one uses the correct HTTP verb for its message.
questions.explanation: Each Route:: method is named after its HTTP verb: post, put, patch, delete (and get).

questions.text: What do named routes allow you to do?
options: Generate URLs or redirects for specific routes easily
questions.explanation: Slide: "Named routes allow you to generate URLs or redirects for specific routes easily."

questions.text: Complete the named route and the URL generation from the slides.
questions.explanation: Chain ->name('profile') to name the route, then use the route('profile') helper to generate its URL.

questions.text: Given Route::get('/profile', ...)->name('profile');, what does route('profile') return?
options: The URL for that route, e.g. http://127.0.0.1:8000/profile
The output of the profile page
questions.explanation: The route() helper generates the (full) URL for a named route.

questions.text: Why are named routes useful when a URL path later changes (e.g. /profile becomes /my-account)?
options: Named routes cannot be changed at all
The old URL keeps working forever automatically
You must search and replace every link in every view
You change the path once in the route definition; every route('profile') call keeps working
questions.explanation: This is the "Route Handling" benefit from Module 1: route names can be changed in one place via a dedicated file.

questions.text: In Route::get('/profile', [UserController::class, 'show'])->name('profile');, what handles the request?
questions.explanation: The array [UserController::class, 'show'] points the route to UserController's show method. 'profile' is only the route's name.

questions.text: What are route parameters used for?
options: Defining dynamic routes (capturing parts of the URL)
questions.explanation: Slide: "Define dynamic routes using parameters."

questions.text: Match each route parameter syntax to its meaning.
allChoices: Regular expression constraint
Optional parameter
Required parameter
Named route
questions.explanation: A ? after the parameter name makes it optional. Give the closure's variable a default value.

questions.text: What does visiting /user/5 return?
questions.context:
Route::get('/user/{id}', function ($id) {
    return 'User '.$id;
});
questions.explanation: {id} captures 5, and 'User '.$id concatenates it into "User 5".

questions.text: What does visiting /user (no name given) return?
questions.context:
Route::get('/user/{name?}', function ($name = 'Guest') {
    return 'User '.$name;
});
questions.explanation: {name?} is optional; when missing, $name falls back to its default value 'Guest'.

questions.text: Using the same optional-parameter route, what does visiting /user/Maria return?
questions.context:
Route::get('/user/{name?}', function ($name = 'Guest') {
    return 'User '.$name;
});
questions.explanation: When the parameter is given, it replaces the default.

questions.text: Make the name parameter optional.
questions.explanation: Put a ? after the parameter name: {name?}.

questions.text: When you make a route parameter optional ({name?}), what must you also do?
options: Give the route's corresponding variable a default value (e.g. $name = 'Guest')
questions.explanation: The Laravel docs say: "Make sure to give the route's corresponding variable a default value". If you don't, the closure has nothing to receive when the parameter is missing.

questions.text: In 'User '.$id, what does the . operator do in PHP?
questions.explanation: In PHP, . is the string concatenation operator. (-> accesses object properties, + adds numbers.)

questions.text: Which method constrains the format of route parameters?
questions.explanation: Slide: "You may constrain the format of your route parameters using the where method on a route instance."

questions.text: What two arguments does the where method accept?
options: The controller class and the method name
The name of the parameter and a regular expression defining how it should be constrained
The HTTP verb and the URL
The view name and its data
questions.explanation: Slide: "The where method accepts the name of the parameter and a regular expression…"

questions.text: With ->where('id', '[0-9]+') on /user/{id}, which URLs match the route? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: [0-9]+ means one or more digits and nothing else. Letters and the minus sign don't match, so those URLs give a 404. (Checked with PHP preg_match against the anchored pattern.)

questions.text: With ->where('slug', '[a-zA-Z0-9\-]+') on /post/{slug}, which URLs match? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Only letters, digits, and hyphens are allowed. Underscores and dots aren't in the character set, so those URLs give a 404. (Checked with PHP preg_match.)

questions.text: Why does /post/my_first_post return a 404 error on this route?
questions.context:
Route::get('/post/{slug}', function ($slug) {
    return 'Post Slug: ' . $slug;
})->where('slug', '[a-zA-Z0-9\-]+');
options: The underscore _ is not in the allowed character set
questions.explanation: Slide: "/post/my_first_post (invalid, 404 error)". The allowed set is letters, digits, and hyphen only.

questions.text: What happens when you visit /user/abc with this route?
questions.context:
Route::get('/user/{id}', function ($id) {
    return 'User ID: ' . $id;
})->where('id', '[0-9]+');
questions.explanation: Slide: "/user/abc (invalid, 404 error)". abc doesn't match [0-9]+.

questions.text: With ->where('name', '[A-Za-z]+'), which values of {name} are accepted? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: [A-Za-z]+ allows only upper- and lowercase letters, one or more. Digits and underscores fail.

questions.text: In the regex [0-9]+, what does the + mean?
options: One or more of the preceding characters
questions.explanation: + is a quantifier meaning "one or more". So [0-9]+ means one or more digits.

questions.text: In [a-zA-Z0-9\-], why is the hyphen written as \-?
options: The backslash escapes it so it means a literal hyphen, not a character range
It is a PHP string concatenation
questions.explanation: Inside a character class, - normally means a range (like a-z). Escaping it as \- makes it a literal hyphen.

questions.text: If a route parameter fails its where constraint, Laravel returns a 404 error.
questions.explanation: Both constraint slides show invalid URLs giving a 404 error.

questions.text: Where do you typically place the fallback route?
options: At the end of your route definitions
questions.explanation: Slide: "You typically place this route at the end of your route definitions to ensure it catches any requests that haven't been handled by previous routes."

questions.text: What is the purpose of a fallback route?
options: To catch any request that no other route handled
To redirect every request to the home page
questions.explanation: The fallback route runs when no other route matches the incoming request.

questions.text: Complete the fallback route from the slides.
questions.explanation: Route::fallback(...) defines the catch-all route.

questions.text: In response()->view('errors.404', [], 404), match each argument to its meaning.
allChoices: The HTTP status code
Data passed to the view (none here)
The view to render

pairs.match: Data passed to the view (none here)

questions.explanation: response()->view($view, $data, $status): the view name, an array of data for it, and the HTTP status code.

questions.text: Which file does the view name 'errors.404' refer to?
questions.explanation: In view names, dots stand for folder separators: errors.404 → resources/views/errors/404.blade.php.

questions.text: The Routes chapter outline lists Route Groups. Using the study plan's example, what URL reaches the dashboard?
questions.context:
Route::prefix('admin')->group(function () {
    Route::get('/dashboard', function () { return 'Admin dashboard'; });
    Route::get('/settings', function () { return 'Admin settings'; });
});
questions.explanation: Route::prefix('admin') adds /admin in front of every route inside the group.

questions.text: Complete the route group so both routes live under /admin.
questions.explanation: Route::prefix('admin')->group(function () { ... }).

questions.text: In this group, what is the full name of the first route?
questions.context:
Route::prefix('users')->name('users.')->group(function () {
    Route::get('/', [UserController::class, 'index'])->name('index');
    Route::get('/create', [UserController::class, 'create'])->name('create');
});
questions.explanation: ->name('users.') puts users. in front of every route name inside the group, so ->name('index') becomes users.index.

questions.text: What is the purpose of route caching?
options: To cache the routes for faster application load time in production
questions.explanation: Slide: "Improving Performance: Cache the routes for faster application load time in production."

questions.text: Complete the Artisan commands to cache routes and then clear the route cache.
questions.code:
php artisan route:___
php artisan route:___
questions.explanation: php artisan route:cache builds the cache; php artisan route:clear removes it.

questions.text: Your routes are cached and you add a new route to routes/web.php. What should you do?
options: Generate a fresh route cache (run route:cache again) or clear it with route:clear
Nothing; Laravel picks up new routes automatically
questions.explanation: Laravel docs: "if you add any new routes you will need to generate a fresh route cache." The cached file is loaded on every request, so new routes are ignored until you rebuild it.

questions.text: In which environment is route caching recommended?
questions.explanation: The slide says to cache routes "for faster application load time in production." The docs recommend running it during deployment.

questions.text: Match each routing best practice to its advice.
allChoices: Group related routes and use route names effectively
Always validate input in routes to prevent security vulnerabilities
Use consistent naming conventions for routes

pairs.match: Use consistent naming conventions for routes
Group related routes and use route names effectively
Always validate input in routes to prevent security vulnerabilities

questions.explanation: From the Best Practices for Routing slide.

questions.text: According to the best practices slide, why should you always validate input in routes?
questions.explanation: Slide: "Security: Always validate input in routes to prevent security vulnerabilities."

questions.text: The study plan recommends a naming convention for routes like users.index and users.show. What is this style called?
questions.explanation: Route names like users.index use dot notation. It matches the redirect()->route('users.index') calls in the controller.

questions.text: Which topics are in the Laravel Routes chapter outline? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Chapter outline: What is Routes?, Basic Routing, Route Parameter, Fallback Route, Route Groups, Route Cache.

questions.text: What do views separate?
options: Your controller/application logic from your presentation logic
questions.explanation: Slide: "Views separate your controller / application logic from your presentation logic."

questions.text: Where are views stored?
questions.explanation: Views live in the resources/views directory.

questions.text: View templates are usually written using which templating language?
questions.explanation: Slide: "view templates are usually written using the Blade templating language."

questions.text: Which file extension marks a Blade template?
questions.explanation: Blade files end in .blade.php, e.g. greeting.blade.php.

questions.text: What does the .blade.php extension tell the framework?
options: That the file contains a Blade template
That the file is a controller
That the file should be served as static HTML
That the file is a migration
questions.explanation: Slide: "The .blade.php extension informs the framework that the file contains a Blade template."

questions.text: According to the slides, Blade directives let you easily… (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Slide: "Blade templates contain HTML as well as Blade directives that allow you to easily echo values, create 'if' statements, iterate over data, and more."

questions.text: Blade templates can contain HTML as well as Blade directives.
questions.explanation: Slide: "Blade templates contain HTML as well as Blade directives…"

questions.text: Complete the Artisan command that creates a new view named greeting.
questions.explanation: php artisan make:view greeting.

questions.text: What file does php artisan make:view greeting create?
questions.explanation: Views go in resources/views and use the .blade.php extension.

questions.text: Which global helper returns a view from a route or controller?
questions.explanation: Slide: "…you may return it from one of your application's routes or controllers using the global view helper."

questions.text: In view('greeting', ['name' => 'James']), what is the second argument?
options: An array of data that becomes available as variables in the view ($name)
questions.explanation: The data array's keys become variables in the view. 'name' => 'James' gives you $name.

questions.text: What will the browser show?
questions.context:
// routes/web.php
Route::get('/', function () {
    return view('greeting', ['name' => 'James']);
});

{{-- resources/views/greeting.blade.php --}}
Hello, {{ $name }}.
questions.explanation: {{ $name }} echoes the name value passed to the view.

questions.text: Blade prevents you from using plain PHP code in your templates.
questions.explanation: Slide: "Unlike some PHP templating engines, Blade does not restrict you from using plain PHP code in your templates."

questions.text: Why does Blade add "essentially zero overhead" to your application?
options: Blade templates are compiled into plain PHP code and cached until they are modified
Blade templates are converted to static HTML once at install
Blade runs in the browser, not on the server
questions.explanation: Slide: "Blade templates are compiled into plain PHP code and cached until they are modified, meaning Blade adds essentially zero overhead."

questions.text: Combining Modules 1 and 3: where does Laravel keep the compiled Blade templates?
questions.explanation: Module 1 says storage contains "compiled Blade templates". Module 3 says Blade templates are compiled and cached. (Specifically storage/framework/views.)

questions.text: When is a cached compiled Blade template recompiled?
options: Never; you must delete it manually
questions.explanation: Templates are "cached until they are modified."

questions.text: Complete the directives that wrap a block of plain PHP inside a Blade template.
questions.explanation: @php ... @endphp runs a block of plain PHP in the template.

questions.text: What does this Blade snippet display?
questions.context:
@php
    $counter = 1;
@endphp
Counter is {{ $counter }}.
questions.explanation: @php sets $counter = 1, and {{ $counter }} echoes it.

questions.text: How do you display a variable passed to a Blade view?
options: Wrap it in double curly braces: {{ $name }}
<?= $name ?> only; Blade has no echo syntax
questions.explanation: Slide: "You may display data that is passed to your Blade views by wrapping the variable in curly braces."

questions.text: What does The current UNIX timestamp is {{ time() }}. display?
options: The current UNIX timestamp (seconds since Jan 1, 1970)
The current date formatted as YYYY-MM-DD
An error: functions can't be used in {{ }}
questions.explanation: Slide: "You are not limited to displaying the contents of the variables passed to the view. You may also echo the results of any PHP function."

questions.text: Inside a Blade echo statement {{ }}, you can only put variables, not function calls.
questions.explanation: You can echo the result of any PHP function, e.g. {{ time() }}. The slide says you may put any PHP code you wish inside a Blade echo statement.

questions.text: {{ }} output is automatically passed through which PHP function to guard against XSS attacks?
questions.explanation: Blade's {{ }} echo runs output through htmlspecialchars, so HTML/script tags in the data are escaped rather than executed. (Laravel docs, Displaying Data.)

questions.text: Complete the Blade if statement from the slides.
questions.explanation: @if, @elseif, @else, @endif.

questions.text: If $records = ['a', 'b', 'c'], what does this template display?
questions.context:
@if (count($records) === 1)
    I have one record!
@elseif (count($records) > 1)
    I have multiple records!
@else
    I don't have any records!
@endif
questions.explanation: count($records) is 3, which is > 1.

questions.text: If $records = [], what does it display?
questions.context:
@if (count($records) === 1)
    I have one record!
@elseif (count($records) > 1)
    I have multiple records!
@else
    I don't have any records!
@endif
questions.explanation: count([]) is 0. That's neither === 1 nor > 1, so the @else branch runs.

questions.text: If $records = ['only one'], what does it display?
questions.context:
@if (count($records) === 1)
    I have one record!
@elseif (count($records) > 1)
    I have multiple records!
@else
    I don't have any records!
@endif
questions.explanation: count($records) === 1 is true.

questions.text: In count($records) === 1, what does === check?
options: That the value is not equal
Only that the values are loosely equal
That both the value and the type are equal (strict comparison)
questions.explanation: === is PHP's strict (identical) comparison. == is loose comparison, and = is assignment.

questions.text: The study plan suggests passing ['records' => 3] to this view. What actually happens on PHP 8+?
questions.context:
@if (count($records) === 1)
    I have one record!
@elseif (count($records) > 1)
    I have multiple records!
@else
    I don't have any records!
@endif
options: It displays "I don't have any records!"
A TypeError is thrown because count() only accepts an array or Countable, not an int
questions.explanation: Verified with PHP 8.2: count(3) throws "count(): Argument #1 ($value) must be of type Countable|array, int given". Pass an array instead (e.g. ['records' => [1, 2, 3]]) to test each branch.

questions.text: Which directives are used to build a Blade switch statement? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Slide: "Switch statements can be constructed using the @switch, @case, @break, @default and @endswitch directives."

questions.text: If $i = 2, what does this display?
questions.context:
@switch($i)
    @case(1)
        First case...
        @break
    @case(2)
        Second case...
        @break
    @default
        Default case...
@endswitch
questions.explanation: $i matches @case(2), and @break stops before the default.

questions.text: If $i = 7, what does this display?
questions.context:
@switch($i)
    @case(1)
        First case...
        @break
    @case(2)
        Second case...
        @break
    @default
        Default case...
@endswitch
questions.explanation: No case matches 7, so @default runs.

questions.text: The first @break has been removed. If $i = 1, what is displayed?
questions.context:
@switch($i)
    @case(1)
        First case...
    @case(2)
        Second case...
        @break
    @default
        Default case...
@endswitch
questions.explanation: Blade compiles to a normal PHP switch, so without @break execution falls through into case 2 until the next @break. (Checked by running the equivalent PHP switch.)

questions.text: Complete the switch statement.
questions.explanation: @switch(...), @case(...), @break, @default, @endswitch.

questions.text: Complete the Blade loop from the slides.
questions.explanation: @foreach($users as $user) ... @endforeach.

questions.text: In <li>{{ $user->name }}</li>, what does -> do?
options: Accesses the name property of the $user object
questions.explanation: -> is PHP's object property/method access operator.

questions.text: If $users = ['Ana', 'Bo', 'Cy'], how many <li> elements are rendered?
questions.context:
<ul>
@foreach ($users as $user)
    <li>{{ $user }}</li>
@endforeach
</ul>
questions.explanation: @foreach runs once per element: Ana, Bo, Cy.

questions.text: What is the syntax for a Blade comment?
questions.explanation: Blade comments use {{-- ... --}}.

questions.text: How are Blade comments different from HTML comments?
options: Blade comments are not included in the HTML returned by your application
Blade comments are shown on the page as text
Blade comments only work inside @php blocks
questions.explanation: Slide: "unlike HTML comments, Blade comments are not included in the HTML returned by your application."

questions.text: An HTML comment <!-- secret note --> written in a Blade view can be seen by anyone who views the page source.
questions.explanation: HTML comments are sent to the browser as part of the HTML. Use {{-- --}} if the comment shouldn't reach the browser.

questions.text: What does CSRF stand for?
questions.explanation: CSRF = Cross-Site Request Forgery, an attack where another site tricks a logged-in user's browser into submitting a request.

questions.text: What does the @csrf directive generate?
options: A hidden CSRF token field in the form
questions.explanation: Slide: "…include a hidden CSRF token field in the form… You may use the @csrf Blade directive to generate the token field."

questions.text: Why should forms include the CSRF token field?
options: So the CSRF protection middleware can validate the request
So the form can use PUT
questions.explanation: Slide: "…so that the CSRF protection middleware can validate the request."

questions.text: According to the slide, when should you include a CSRF token field?
options: Anytime you define an HTML form in your application
questions.explanation: Slide: "Anytime you define an HTML form in your application, you should include a hidden CSRF token field."

questions.text: What is the name of the hidden input that @csrf generates?
questions.explanation: @csrf renders <input type="hidden" name="_token" value="...">.

questions.text: You submit a POST form that is missing @csrf. What does Laravel typically respond with?
questions.explanation: When the CSRF token is missing or doesn't match, Laravel rejects the request with HTTP 419 ("Page Expired").

questions.text: Which HTTP verbs can plain HTML forms not send directly? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Slide: "Since HTML forms can't make PUT, PATCH, or DELETE requests, you will need to add a hidden _method field to spoof these HTTP verbs."

questions.text: What is the name of the hidden field that @method('PUT') creates?
questions.explanation: @method('PUT') renders <input type="hidden" name="_method" value="PUT">.

questions.text: When using @method('PUT'), what should the form's own method attribute be?
options: It doesn't need a method attribute
questions.explanation: The slide's example is <form action="/foo/bar" method="POST"> with @method('PUT') inside. The browser sends a POST, and Laravel reads _method to treat it as PUT.

questions.text: Complete this delete form.
questions.explanation: @csrf adds the token; @method('DELETE') spoofs the DELETE verb.

questions.text: Adding a hidden _method field to make a POST form act as PUT/PATCH/DELETE is called…
questions.explanation: The slide says the _method field is used to "spoof these HTTP verbs". The docs call this Form Method Spoofing.

questions.text: How many hidden inputs does this form's Blade code produce?
questions.context:
<form action="/users/1" method="POST">
    @csrf
    @method('PUT')
    <input type="text" name="name">
</form>
questions.explanation: @csrf gives a hidden _token input and @method('PUT') gives a hidden _method input: 2 in total.

questions.text: Which version of the Laravel documentation does the Views deck reference?
questions.explanation: References slide: https://laravel.com/docs/11.x/.

questions.text: Match each Blade syntax to its purpose.
allChoices: Generates a hidden CSRF token field
Displays (echoes) data
Spoofs PUT/PATCH/DELETE with a hidden _method field
Runs a block of plain PHP
Loops over data
A comment that is not sent to the browser

pairs.match: Generates a hidden CSRF token field
Spoofs PUT/PATCH/DELETE with a hidden _method field
Runs a block of plain PHP
A comment that is not sent to the browser

questions.explanation: All of these come from the Blade Templates section of Module 3.

questions.text: Instead of defining all request handling logic as ______ in your route files, you can organize it using controller classes.
questions.explanation: Slide: "Instead of defining all of your request handling logic as closures in your route files, you may wish to organize this behavior using 'controller' classes."

questions.text: What do controllers do with request handling logic?
options: Group related request handling logic into a single class
Spread it across many route files
questions.explanation: Slide: "Controllers can group related request handling logic into a single class."

questions.text: According to the slides, what might a UserController handle?
options: All incoming requests related to users: showing, creating, updating, and deleting users
questions.explanation: Slide: "…a UserController class might handle all incoming requests related to users, including showing, creating, updating, and deleting users."

questions.text: By default, where are controllers stored?
questions.explanation: Slide: "By default, controllers are stored in the app/Http/Controllers directory."

questions.text: Complete the Artisan command that generates a new controller.
questions.explanation: php artisan make:controller UserController.

questions.text: In php artisan make:controller UserController, what is UserController?
questions.explanation: The slide labels it "Controller Name".

questions.text: How many public methods can a controller have?
questions.explanation: Slide: "A controller may have any number of public methods which will respond to incoming HTTP requests."

questions.text: What is the namespace of the controllers in the slides?
questions.explanation: namespace App\Http\Controllers; matches the folder app/Http/Controllers.

questions.text: In class UserController extends Controller, what does extends Controller mean?
questions.explanation: extends is PHP class inheritance. UserController gets everything the base Controller class provides.

questions.text: In public function show(string $id): View, what does : View mean?
questions.context:
<?php

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Models\User;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class UserController extends Controller
{
    /**
     * Show the profile for a given user.
     */
    public function show(string $id): View
    {
        return view('user.profile', [
            'user' => User::findOrFail($id)
        ]);
    }
}
options: It means the parameter is a view
It's the method's return type: it must return an Illuminate\View\View
questions.explanation: : View is a return-type declaration. The class View is imported with use Illuminate\View\View;.

questions.text: What happens if User::findOrFail($id) can't find a user with that ID?
questions.context:
<?php

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Models\User;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class UserController extends Controller
{
    /**
     * Show the profile for a given user.
     */
    public function show(string $id): View
    {
        return view('user.profile', [
            'user' => User::findOrFail($id)
        ]);
    }
}
options: It returns null and the view shows blank
Laravel throws a ModelNotFoundException, which becomes a 404 response
It creates a new empty user
It returns the first user instead
questions.explanation: findOrFail throws ModelNotFoundException when there's no match, and Laravel turns that into a 404. Plain find() would return null.

questions.text: Which file does view('user.profile', ...) render?
questions.explanation: The dot in user.profile means a subfolder: user/profile.blade.php.

questions.text: Inside the user.profile view, which variable holds the user?
questions.context:
<?php

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Models\User;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class UserController extends Controller
{
    /**
     * Show the profile for a given user.
     */
    public function show(string $id): View
    {
        return view('user.profile', [
            'user' => User::findOrFail($id)
        ]);
    }
}
questions.explanation: The array key 'user' becomes the $user variable in the view.

questions.text: Complete the route that points to the controller's show method.
questions.explanation: UserController::class gives the fully qualified class name. The array syntax is [ClassName::class, 'methodName'].

questions.text: What does UserController::class evaluate to?
questions.explanation: ::class returns the fully qualified class name as a string.

questions.text: Which use statement must be at the top of routes/web.php to reference UserController::class by its short name?
questions.explanation: The slide imports it with use App\Http\Controllers\UserController;.

questions.text: For Route::get('/user/{id}', [UserController::class, 'show']);, how does show() receive the ID?
options: It must read the ID from the session
It can't; controllers don't get route parameters
The {id} route parameter is passed to the method's $id argument
questions.explanation: Route parameters are passed to the controller method's arguments, the same way they're passed to closures.

allChoices: Show the form for creating a new user
Update the specified user in storage

Remove the specified user from storage

questions.text: Drag each HTTP verb + URI to the controller method it maps to (from the study plan's routes).
questions.explanation: Study plan Session 4.5 route list. These are also the standard Laravel resource routes.

questions.text: What does User::all() in the index method do?
options: Retrieves all users from the database
questions.explanation: User::all() is Eloquent; it returns every row in the users table as a collection.

questions.text: What is compact('users') equivalent to?
questions.explanation: compact() builds an array from variable names. Checked with PHP: compact('users') returns ['users' => $users].

questions.text: In store(), what happens if $request->validate([...]) fails?
options: PHP crashes with a fatal error
Laravel automatically redirects back with the validation errors; the rest of the method doesn't run
The invalid user is saved anyway
questions.explanation: When validation fails, Laravel throws a validation exception and redirects back with the errors (and old input). User::create is never reached.

questions.text: In store(), which validation rules are applied to email? (Select all that apply)
questions.context:
$validatedData = $request->validate([
    'name' => 'required|string|max:255',
    'email' => 'required|string|email|max:255|unique:users',
]);
questions.explanation: 'email' => 'required|string|email|max:255|unique:users'.

questions.text: What does the unique:users rule check?
options: That the email doesn't already exist in the users table
That the user is logged in
That only one field was submitted
That the email is spelled correctly
questions.explanation: unique:users checks the users table for an existing row with the same value.

questions.text: What does max:255 mean for a string field?
questions.explanation: For strings, max:255 limits the length to 255 characters.

questions.text: In update(), why is the rule 'unique:users,email,' . $id instead of just unique:users?
questions.context: 'email' => 'required|string|email|max:255|unique:users,email,' . $id,
options: It checks the ID is unique
It lets duplicate emails through for everyone
It ignores the current user's own row, so they can keep their existing email
questions.explanation: The third part of unique:table,column,id is an ID to ignore. Without it, saving a user with their own unchanged email would fail as "already taken".

questions.text: What does ->with('success', 'User created successfully.') do in the redirect?
options: Writes the message to the database
Flashes a success message to the session for the next request
Adds a query string ?success=... to the URL
Displays the message immediately without redirecting
questions.explanation: redirect()->...->with(key, value) flashes data to the session. It's available on the next page, e.g. to show a success alert.

questions.text: Where does redirect()->route('users.index') send the user?
options: To the URL of the route named users.index (the users list)
questions.explanation: redirect()->route('name') redirects to a named route's URL. This is why the study plan names every route (users.index, etc.).

questions.text: Which CRUD methods on the slides end with a redirect instead of returning a view? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: store, update, and destroy change data and then redirect()->route('users.index')->with(...). The others return views.

questions.text: Which CRUD methods on the slides call User::findOrFail($id)? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Every method that works on one existing user looks it up with findOrFail. index lists all users, create just shows a form, and store makes a new user.

questions.text: Match each Eloquent call to what it does in the CRUD controller.
allChoices: Save changes to an existing user
Remove the user
Get every user
Insert a new user

pairs.match: Save changes to an existing user

questions.explanation: The Eloquent calls used in index, store, update, and destroy.

questions.text: Which class is type-hinted in store(Request $request), and where is it imported from?
questions.explanation: The CRUD controller imports use Illuminate\Http\Request;.

questions.text: What is the full namespace of the User model used in the controllers?
questions.explanation: The slides import use App\Models\User;. (Laravel 7 and older used App\User.)

questions.text: Which method signature does update use on the slides?
questions.explanation: update needs both the submitted form data ($request) and which user to change ($id).

questions.text: Which view does the CRUD controller's show($id) return?
questions.explanation: In the full CRUD slides, show returns view('users.show', compact('user')). The earlier single-method example used user.profile.

questions.text: The study plan lists /users/create before /users/{id}. Why is that order a good idea?
options: create must always be the first route in the file
Laravel requires routes to be in alphabetical order
Order has no effect in any case
Otherwise /users/{id} (with no constraint) could match /users/create and treat "create" as an ID
questions.explanation: Uncached routes are matched in the order they're defined. An unconstrained {id} accepts any text, including create. Putting the specific route first (or adding ->where('id', '[0-9]+')) avoids this.

questions.text: In the study plan's edit form, which combination of directives and action is used?
options: No directives; forms can send PUT directly
questions.explanation: The edit form POSTs to users.update with @method('PUT') to spoof PUT and @csrf for the token.

questions.text: If you follow the slides' store() exactly on Laravel's default users table (which has a required password column), what happens when you submit only name and email?
options: Laravel generates a random password automatically
The user is created with an empty password
The insert fails with a database error, because password can't be NULL
questions.explanation: The default users migration has a non-nullable password column, and the store() rules only validate/pass name and email. To make the study plan's end-to-end test work, add a password field (hashed) or make the column nullable.

questions.text: Match each prerequisite check (Session 0) to its command.
allChoices: npm start
php -v
php artisan -v
node -v
composer -V

questions.text: After php artisan serve, which URL shows the default Laravel welcome page?
questions.explanation: php artisan serve starts a local dev server at http://127.0.0.1:8000 by default.

questions.text: For the simplest local database setup, what does the study plan suggest?
options: Set DB_CONNECTION=sqlite in .env and create an empty database/database.sqlite file
questions.explanation: Session 4.1: switch DB_CONNECTION=sqlite and create database/database.sqlite.

questions.text: Which file holds your database credentials?
questions.explanation: The .env file holds environment settings like DB_CONNECTION, DB_DATABASE, DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD.

questions.text: What does php artisan migrate do?
options: Moves the project to another folder
Runs the database migrations, creating tables like users
Updates Laravel to the newest version
questions.explanation: Migrations (in database/migrations) define the tables; migrate applies them.

questions.text: What is php artisan tinker?
options: An interactive shell (REPL) for running PHP/Laravel code against your app
questions.explanation: Tinker lets you run code like User::create([...]) or route('profile') interactively.

questions.text: In User::create([... 'password' => bcrypt('password')]), what does bcrypt() do?
options: Hashes the password before it's stored
questions.explanation: bcrypt() hashes the password. This is the "password hashing" security feature from Module 1.

questions.text: Your study plan says route:cache cannot cache closure routes. According to the Laravel 11.x documentation (the version the Views deck references), is that still true?
options: Yes, and controller routes can't be cached either
Route caching was removed in Laravel 11
No. That limitation is from older versions (Laravel 7 and earlier); the 11.x docs no longer mention it
questions.explanation: The Laravel 7.x docs say "Closure based routes cannot be cached." The 11.x routing docs have no such restriction; closure routes are serialized when cached. Pointing routes at controller methods is still good organization.

questions.text: Which of these are real Artisan commands used in these modules / the study plan? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Routes are written by hand in routes/web.php. There's no make:route, and views are created with make:view, not view:create.

pairs.match: Creates a new Blade view file
Caches routes for faster load time

questions.text: In a Laravel project, the View part of MVC corresponds to…
questions.explanation: Views are Blade templates in resources/views.

questions.text: A route can return a view directly from a closure, without using a controller.
questions.explanation: E.g. Route::get('/welcome', function () { return view('welcome'); });. Controllers are optional, but recommended for organizing larger apps.

questions.text: Which flow correctly describes how the /users list page is produced in the CRUD app?
questions.explanation: The route sends the request to the controller. The controller asks the Model for data, then hands it to the View to render.

questions.text: Put these in the order a request flows through: (1) Blade view renders HTML, (2) route matches the URL, (3) controller method runs, (4) Eloquent model queries the DB.
questions.explanation: Route matches, then the controller runs, then the model gets data, then the view renders it.

questions.text: A form in users/create.blade.php should submit a new user. Which is correct?
options: <form method="GET" action="{{ route('users.store') }}"> with no directives
questions.explanation: store is a POST route named users.store, and every form needs @csrf.

questions.text: Route::fallback(...) must be named with ->name('fallback') to work.
questions.explanation: The fallback route works without a name. Route::fallback() registers it as the catch-all on its own.

questions.text: The where method is used to constrain route parameters with regular expressions, while $request->validate() is used to validate submitted form data in controllers.
questions.explanation: where limits which URLs match a route. validate() checks form input such as required|email|unique:users.

questions.text: Which of these correctly returns the errors.404 view with a 404 status from the fallback route?
questions.explanation: response()->view($view, $data, $status) returns the view with a custom status code, exactly as on the Fallback Route slide.
